lectures.title: Multimedia Computing: Concepts and Definitions
lectures.content: Outline • What is Multimedia • The Convergence of Multimedia Technologies • Multimedia Data Sources • Multimodal Interactions • Multimedia Big Data • Artificial Intelligence for Multimedia • Multimedia Communications and Networking • Multimedia Technologies Convergence and Cybersecurity • Applications of Multimedia Technologies Objectives of the Course • At the end of the course, YOU will be able to: – Have an excellent understanding of Multimedia: • Technologies • Services • Applications – Understand the different traditional and emerging Media – Master basic networking concepts and protocols – Understand how multimedia and networking (communications) play together – Master the Digital Twin concept, and the convergence of its enabling technologies Definition: Multimedia • Notion – Multi • Many – Media • "Things in the middle" • These media can be in the form of: • Graphics, animation, audio, video, text, haptics, smell, etc. – by • Computer, TV, phone, etc. Multimedia Applications • Multimedia application can be either linear or non-linear • Linear – Not interactive – Starting at a beginning and running through the end • Eg. Montage on TV • Non-linear – Interactive – Ability of end user to interact and control the application • Eg. Games software Multimedia Interpretations • Perception: How do humans perceive Information? – aural sense, visual sense • Representation (Computer Science): How is information coded? – ASCII, GIF, JPEG, ... • Presentation (in Electronics): Which ‘medium’ is used to convey (I/O) info? – paper, monitor, loudspeaker, .. • Storage (for Publishers): Where is information stored? – paper, Hard disk, CD-ROM, ... • Transmission (in Data Communication): Which ‘medium’ is used to transmit info.? – coaxial, optical fiber, .. • Distribution (for Content Providers): Which ‘medium’ is used to exchange info? – CD, JAZ-Drives, optical fiber, ... • Dissemination (in Public): which ‘medium’ conveys info to the public? – Press, TV, Radio, (coming: Internet): term "mass media" coined in 1923 Multimedia Systems Y Combination of: This is plain text Spread Sheet Discrete Media X & Y T Continuous Media X Multimedia Communications • MULTIMEDIA COMMUNICATIONS is the field referring to the: – Representation, – Storage, – Retrieval, and – Dissemination • of – Machine-processable information expressed in multiple media such as: • Text, Voice, Graphics, Images, Animations, Audio, Video, smell and touch Multimedia is everywhere MULTIMEDIA DATA PRESENTATION Used in almost every field: Education; Entertainment; Marketing; Healthcare; Military, etc. Multimedia Content • Exists in different formats, we are aware o: – Text, Audio and Video • Content processing devices can – Capture – Access – Play / Display – Interact with the multimedia content Definition: Haptics • Haptics: a technology that can create an experience of touch. This includes vibrations, forces, motion, etc. Device Actuator Haptic jacket Haptic Force-Feedback Haptic Arm Band Haptic Glove Vibrating Sofa El Saddik, A., Orozco, M., Eid, M., & Cha, J. (2011). Haptics technologies: Bringing touch to multimedia. Springer. Multimedia content IoT Social Networks Medical Finance Multimedia Data Sources • Sensors (Hardware sensors): A sensor is a device which detects or measures a physical property and sends the information to other electronics. • Increasing use of sensors: Sensors Actuators IOT Examples of Sensors • Just in a smartphone: – Global Positioning System (GPS) – Accelerometer – Sound Sensor (Microphone) – Magnetometer (compass) – Proximity sensor – Ambient Light Sensor – Barometer Sensor Sensors – Touchscreen Sensors – Fingerprint Sensor – Heart Rate Sensor Actuators – Pedometer IOT – Barcode Sensor – Gyroscope – More ! lectures.title: Multimedia Computing: Compression
lectures.content: Outline • Motivation • Requirements - General • Fundamentals - Categories • Coding • Image Compression – JPEG – JPEG2000 • Video Compression – Video Compression Concepts – MPEG-Family • Conclusion Introduction • Recently, more and more data is being collected in huge amounts, and at a high velocity, coming from all sort of different sources. • This data has the potential to give insights to business and governments more than ever before • At the same time, dealing with such data can be very challenging and many research areas are related to solving these challenges. Big Data Definition “Big data is a field that treats ways to analyze, systematically extract information from, or otherwise deal with data sets that are too large or complex to be dealt with by traditional data-processing application software” – Wikipedia Big Data 5 V’s The Big Data 5 V’s : • 3 key concepts that describe how big data is different than regular data: – Volume – Variety – Velocity • 2 more V’s have emerged, that are important to Big Data: – Value – Veracity Big Data Statistics • “Worldwide Big Data market revenues for software and services are projected to increase from $42B in 2018 to $103B in 2027” Forbes. Big Data Volume & Variety • Approximately 402.74 million terabytes of data are created each day • Around 147 zettabytes of data will be generated this year • 181 zettabytes of data will be generated in 2025 – Videos account for over half of internet data traffic • According to the latest estimates, 402.74 million terabytes of data are created each day. – Video 53.72% – Social 12.69% – Gaming 9.86% – Web browsing 5.67% – Messaging 5.35% – Marketplace 4.54% – File sharing 3.74% – Etc. Big Data Volume (cont.) Acumen Research and Consulting recently published report titled “Big Data Market and Region Forecast, 2022 - 2030”, December 15, 2022 Big Data Variety • Multiple data sources: – Data generated by humans or by machines • Various forms: – Structured. Example: data tables, relational databases (defined schema), – Semi structured. Example: XML, JSON. – Unstructured data. Example: audio, image, video • Classify this data into different categories Big Data Velocity • Data is accumulated at high speed • Processing this data has to be timely • Real time results / near real time results are sometimes needed Source: Edureka Value • How can we get value from Big Data • Extract useful information from this data • Keep all the data vs. get rid of “unuseful” data ? – How to determine unuseful / useful data? – In the health domain, vital signs data is very valuable – For the Digital Twin: we want to keep the data to build the DT including the full history • Analysis: AI plays a very important role, because large volume of data is only as useful as the information you can extract from it • AI is not the only player: domain experts and insightful analysts who know what to look for and who can recognize patterns Veracity • How truthful and how reliable is the collected data • Inconsistencies exist in the collected data • Loosing data packets lost/corrupted along the huge amount of data transfer • This results in missing/inconsistent values in the data ? Advantages of Big Data • The Big Data real benefits come from analyzing it, which allows discovering patterns that are advantageous in many fields • Better decisions • Competitiveness • Growth opportunities • Customer loyalty and retention • Understanding market conditions • Influence online reputation • Etc…

lectures.title: Multimedia Computing: Multimedia Interactions
lectures.content: Introduction • Multimodality in human-computer interactions combines interactions using more than one mode of communication • Multimodal interfaces use a wide range of software and hardware devices, to achieve higher degrees of immersion and more efficient interaction. Ecosystem of the Digital Twin for health and well-being. Published in IEEE MMTC Communications – Frontiers. “Dtwins: A Digital Twins Ecosystem For Health And Well-Being” by El Saddik et al. Definitions • Multimodal Interaction refers to the use of more than one modality to communicate. • A modality here is a channel by which information is communicated between the computer and the human Multimedia Interactions: Mostly 3 Senses • Vision – Via human eyes and most information rich media – Humans perceive between 0.3 and 0.7 microns wavelength – Temporal and spatial limitations define visual displays • Audition – Via human ears and very effective – Humans perceive 16 Hz to 20000Hz (1000Hz and 4000Hz) – Auditory interfaces are very mature (2D and 3D sound effects) • Touch – Distributed all over the human body, up to 1 KHz sensitivity – Tactile and kinesthetic – Bi-directional flow of information and energy Advanced Media • Conventional media: audio, video, text, image, … • Emerging types of media provide greater interaction. • Wearable/enhanced interfaces – Head-Mounted Displays – 3D Goggles – Gloves – Haptics (e-touch) – Others … • The high-level of immersion and interaction with these new devices and media can lead to unprecedented rich learning experience. From regular images to Panoramas • Navigable images – A single-image immersive environment • Very effective for learning – Historic site – Museums – History –… Context Sensitive Panoramas • Panoramas that show additional information depending on the context. • User can focus on a specific learning object to get information about it. • There are many ways this “focus” can happen: – click – markers – gaze recognition – gesture recognition • https://www.historymuseum.ca/history-hall/virtual-tour/ Context Sensitive Panoramas Virtual Worlds • 3D Virtual Environments; Virtual Reality based worlds • The idea is to give the impression to the user that what is being experienced is virtually “real”. • We haven’t reached that yet, but in some cases we can offer a somewhat believable experience. • Some believe this can be as simple as having a 3D model on the monitor, made in VRML for example. • The experience is the key: without it, it’s not “real”. • For this experience, we need additional equipment: – HMD – Stereo Goggles – Force-feedback tools – … 3D Worlds avatars 3D Model • Can be created in two ways: – Programming the model, usually with an authoring tool. – 3D scanning of an actual object/scenario. • The resulting 3D model can be stored in a standard format, such as the Virtual Reality Modeling Language (VRML) or X3D. 3D Capturing • Similar to scanning normal 2D images, one can also scan an object to create a 3D model of it. – Medical imaging (MRI, X-Rays, Ultrasounds) – 3D animations (3D Studios) – Computer simulations • Example seen previously: Caves Caves (…) Simulator 3D Video • Stereo view of a video, with or without free viewpoint • Free viewpoint: similar to the concept of panoramas as applied to images, but applied to videos. • On its own or merged with synthetic 3D environment • Potentially very large data sets •Example of 3D 360 video VR: Make sure you look around the video using the mouse. 3D Video System 3D Video Capturing ⚫ Multiple spatially calibrated video cameras using image processing techniques ⚫ This was used at Discover lab while working on an eLearning

lectures.title: Multimedia Computing: Digital Twins & AI-Powered Metaverses
lectures.content: Introduction to 3D GANs • Success of 2D GANs in image synthesis. • Demand for 3D Content Importance in VR, gaming, medical imaging, and Metaverse. • Challenges with Traditional 3D Methods are resource-intensiveness and limitations of engines like OpenGL. From 2D to 3D - The Technological Leap • Volumetric Convolutional Networks Introduction and breakthrough by ShapeNet. • Development of early 3D GANs with more architectural evolution and improvements in model reconstruction capabilities. Generator of the early 3D-GAN 3D Content Generation Explicit Representation in 3D Content Generation • Describes tangible, well-defined geometric structures. • Focuses on direct manipulation of spatial elements like voxels, point clouds, and meshes. ◦ Voxel Grids: ◦ Consists of a 3D grid where each voxel represents a cubic volume in space. ◦ Useful for volumetric analysis but can be memory intensive. • Point Clouds: • A collection of vertices in a three-dimensional coordinate system. • Generated by 3D scanners, offering detailed surface capture. • Meshes: • Composed of vertices, edges, and faces forming polygonal shapes. • Ideal for creating detailed and complex 3D models with high accuracy. Applications in Metaverse: • Virtual real estate uses meshes for creating intricate architectural designs. • Avatar creation uses point clouds for detailed character modeling. 3D Content Generation Implicit Representation in 3D Content Generation • Models complex geometries as continuous functions. • Focuses on properties and fields rather than discrete structures. ◦ Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF): ◦ Consists of a 3D grid where each voxel represents a cubic volume in space. ◦ Enables highly realistic rendering by simulating how light interacts with surfaces. • Generative Radiance Fields (GRAF) and π-GAN: • Extends NeRF by adding control over shape and appearance via adversarial networks. • Allows generation of novel scenes from unposed images. • Enhance realism in virtual environments. Applications in Metaverse: • Capable of producing photo-realistic textures and lighting. • Supports dynamic environment generation with seamless transitions. NeRF GRAF 3D Content Generation Progress of 3D GANs S2-GAN Point-E HoloGAN GRAF IM-Net ShapeGF Pi-GAN H EG3D H H RenderDiffusion 3D-GAN VON PointFlow PolyGen GIRAFFE Get3D Voxel grid Depth Mesh Neural field 3D Representation H Hybrid Points cloud GAN RODIN Autoregressive Energy-based model DiffRF Normalizing Flow Diffusion Generative models Existing tools for 3D GAN Lumalabs: • Specializes in developing advanced 3D modeling technologies utilizing artificial intelligence. • Offers tools for creating highly interactive, realistic 3D scenes and objects that can be embedded and shared easily across web and mobile platforms. • Sponsored by LUMA AI • Link: https://lumalabs.ai/ Nerfstudio: • Nerfstudio provides a simple API that allows for a simplified end-to-end process of creating, training, and testing NeRFs. • Sponsored by LUMA AI and BAIR • Link: https://docs.nerf.studio/ Challenges in 3D Content Generation • High Computational Cost: 3D GANs require significant computational resources due to the complexity of processing three-dimensional data. • Data Availability and Quality: The effectiveness of 3D GANs is heavily dependent on the availability of high-quality, diverse training datasets. • Mode Collapse: A common issue where the generator produces limited varieties of outputs, failing to capture the diversity of the input data. • Multi-View Consistency: Ensuring that generated 3D objects look realistic from all viewpoints is challenging. • Integration with Existing Systems: Difficulty in integrating 3D GANs with current platforms and technologies, especially those not originally designed to support AI-driven models. lectures.title: Multimedia Computing: Quality of Experience
lectures.content: Outline • Introduction • Motivational scenario • Quality of service • Why QoS is not enough ? • Multimedia Evolution • Quality of experience • QoE Measurement Approaches • QoE Modeling • Summary Quality – a simple yet difficult concept Like many human sensations quality is easy to understand but difficult to define According to Wikipedia: A quality (from Latin - qualitas) is an attribute or a property. Some philosophers assert that a quality cannot be defined. In contemporary philosophy, the idea of qualities and especially how to distinguish certain kinds of qualities from one another remains controversial. Measurement Objective: Subjective: Measurable and verifiable aspect of a thing or phenomenon, expressed in numbers or quantities, such as lightness or heaviness, thickness or thinness, softness or hardness. Attribute, characteristic, or property of a thing or phenomenon that can be observed and interpreted, and may be approximated (quantified) but cannot be measured, such as beauty, feel, flavor, taste. Definition according to ISO 9000 • ISO 9000: a family of standards for quality management systems • Quality of something can be determined by comparing a set of inherent characteristics with a set of requirements – High quality: if characteristics meet requirements – Low quality: if characteristics do not meet all requirements • Quality is a relative concept – Degree of quality Quality – is in fact an elephant The blind men and the elephant: Poem by John Godfrey Saxe The blind men and the elephant: Poem by John Godfrey Saxe[13] Perceived quality of a multimedia • Multimedia applications deal with signals that are meant for human consumption and interaction. • To do so, these signals go through many processing stages such as: – Acquisition and processing. – Coding and transmission. – Enhancement and restitution. • These stages may affect the quality of the multimedia presentation and introduce certain artifacts that will disrupt the experience of observer. • Other end-to-end issues including delays in the interactions, usability, human factors, and context related factors can also impact on the multimedia experience by end users. (Example) Experimental testbed Video Server Loss, Delay, Jitter Video Client + Quality Meter Video Characteristics: MPEG2 Bit Rate: ~4Mbps (Example) High Quality Throughput: 5.0 Mbps (Example) Medium Quality Throughput: 3.8 Mbps (Example) Low Quality Throughput: 3 Mbps (Examples) User perception of response times 50 ms 1s 5s Therefor, there are increasing demands to define a set of rules that ensure the quality of multimedia presentation. What is the solution? Quality of service • Service providers have addressed the disrupting issues by the notion of Quality of Service QoS that objectively measures and guarantees service-related characteristics multimedia content from the provider perspective. • QoS has been defined in the IETF RFC 2386: A set of service requirements to be met by the network/system while transporting a flow • Property of the network and its components: refers often to “betterthan-best-effort” packet forwarding. • In general QoS : A collection of performance criteria to measure what degree does the system provide the function it has been built for. Quality of Service (QoS) • ISO standard defines QoS as a concept for specifying how “good” the offered networking services are. • QoS elements: – How to define QoS • Parameter set – How to determine QoS • Negotiation procedure – How to ensure QoS • Reflection in appropriate network access mechanisms (scheduling) • QoS has different implications in different fields: – Operating system / Resource scheduling – File system organization – Compression – Communication system support – Media synchronization – ... – User Interface QOS Framework Application layer e.g. Frame rate, PSNR QOS Network layer

lectures.title: Multimedia Computing: AI in Multimedia
lectures.content: Multimedia Computing ART IF IC IAL IN T EL L IGEN CE IN M U LT IM EDIA Summary of Main Lecture Subjects • What is Artificial Intelligence • Fields of Artificial Intelligence • Paradigms of Machine Learning • Evaluation • Large Language Models • Multimodal AI Artificial Intelligence (AI) • The study and development of computational devices able to perform tasks that usually require human intelligence. • Field of study of how to make computers "smart“. • Technology that enables a machine to simulate human behavior. Source: A. El Saddik Why Artificial Intelligence? • Automate routine work • Security, surveillance • Lower error rate • Too much data to process by a human • Operations that are dangerous to humans • Assistance: virtual assistant, chatbot, virtual medical assistant, food delivery • etc AI and DT • AI: Acting Humanly • AI: Thinking Humanly ? • Can we get the machine intelligence to a point where the Digital Twin can act on behalf of the Real Twin, in a trusted manner? • DT: AI is a foundational DT component. • AI: what have we achieve so far ? Fields of Artificial Intelligence • Humans can communicate naturally using language, and read / write text  Natural language processing (NLP) AI field concerned with programming computers to process natural language data Turing test: Get a human to ask some questions, and a computer to respond. If the human is unable to tell if the responses come from a person or a computer then the natural language processing is successful. Fields of Artificial Intelligence • Humans hear and identify sounds  Sound recognition: AI technology that involves audio signal processing and pattern recognition • Humans can listen and communicate through language  Speech recognition Used in NLP to bypass entering text with a keyboard in order to get it processed. Example: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvbHu_bVa_g Fields of Artificial Intelligence • Humans can see and process what they see  Computer Vision – Humans can recognize scenes  Image Processing Computer Vision • Very popular area of deep learning. • Uses techniques such as: – Image classification, – Object detection, – Object tracking, etc • Used in: – Surveillance: detect suspicious behavior – Face recognition: find you in pictures – Biometrics: fingerprint, face, and iris recognition – Self-deriving cars: detect traffic signs, lights, etc – Gaming, such as Microsoft Kinect games Example: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QcCjmWwEUgg Fields of Artificial Intelligence • Humans move around fluently • Humans also intuitively manipulate objects  Robotics: AI technology that involves moving about and object manipulation Robotics • Two major fields of robotics technology include mobility and manipulation • Mobility and manipulation set robots apart from regular computer systems, as it allows robots to move around and interact with the physical world. • Mobility: motion tracking and visual feedback, obstacle detection, range estimation (distance between me and a target/obstacle) • Manipulation: object recognition, object-independent grasp (unknown objects), task-oriented grasping, tool manipulation Fields of Artificial Intelligence • Humans can detect patterns  Pattern Recognition: using computers in pattern recognition allows handling more data, and many dimensions of data. AI Applications • Autonomous vehicles, such as drones and selfdriving cars • Search engines, such as Google search • Online assistants, such as Siri • Medical diagnosis assistance, such as IBM Watson • Playing games, such as Chess or Go • Online advertisements • Spam filtering • Image recognition Intelligent enough? • Google assistant can make phone calls to book appointments for clients • Store infers what is in the womb from purchases history • Beat best human experts?
